src.t: Psychiatry and Mental Health Curriculum: Year 4 (MKU)

faq.a: Ensure safety, assess for medical causes, then give a rapid‑acting antipsychotic such as intramuscular haloperidol.
faq.q: What is the first step when a patient presents with agitation and possible psychosis?

faq.a: Select a drug that is inexpensive, widely available and has a tolerable side‑effect profile; amitriptyline and fluoxetine are common choices.
faq.q: How do I choose an antidepressant in a low‑resource setting?

faq.a: If there is treatment‑resistant depression, severe suicidality, psychotic features, or comorbid neurological disease.
faq.q: When should I refer a patient with depression to a specialist?

exam: What immediate actions do you take for a patient with acute agitation and a risk of self‑harm? — Secure environment, assess airway, give IM haloperidol, arrange urgent observation.

How would you differentiate depression from hypothyroidism without lab tests? — Look for cold intolerance, weight gain, dry skin; ask about thyroid history; consider trial of antidepressant if unlikely thyroid disease.

A patient with HIV presents with new‑onset psychosis. Which investigations are essential and why? — HIV viral load and CD4 count to assess disease stage; syphilis serology to rule out neurosyphilis; consider brain imaging if focal signs.

Why is haloperidol preferred over chlorpromazine for severe agitation in a low‑resource ward? — Haloperidol has rapid onset, can be given IM, and lower risk of hypotension and anticholinergic side effects.

Explain how you would use the WHO mhGAP guide when a formal psychiatric interview is unavailable. — Follow the stepwise algorithm: screen for danger, assess core symptoms, assign provisional diagnosis, initiate treatment.

What are the red‑flag features that mandate urgent referral for a patient with anxiety symptoms? — Suicidal ideation, panic with chest pain, severe autonomic instability, or coexisting medical emergency.

Describe a brief psychosocial intervention you can deliver in a busy outpatient clinic. — Use problem‑solving therapy: identify problem, brainstorm solutions, set a realistic action plan, schedule follow‑up.
When is it appropriate to avoid benzodiazepines in a patient with anxiety? — In patients with a history of substance misuse, respiratory disease, or when risk of sedation could impair safety.
ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: A concise guide for Year‑4 students to assess, diagnose and manage common mental health disorders in East African hospitals, focusing on limited investigations and practical bedside care.

b: Use WHO mhGAP interview guide when formal psychiatric interview is unavailable
Apply ICD‑11 criteria for common disorders (depression, psychosis, anxiety, substance use)
sections.p: Mental health curriculum outlines the core competencies needed to recognise and diagnose psychiatric disorders using history, mental state examination and locally relevant screening tools.

b: Mild: symptoms present but daily activities largely preserved
Moderate: noticeable impairment, needs outpatient treatment
Severe: marked dysfunction, risk of harm, requires urgent inpatient care
sections.p: Severity is graded by functional impairment and symptom burden; staging guides urgency of referral and intensity of treatment.

b: Infections: HIV, neuro‑tuberculosis, malaria cerebral complications
Chronic disease stress: sickle cell crises, rheumatic heart disease
Substance use: khat, alcohol, cannabis
Psychosocial: trauma, bereavement, poverty, gender‑based violence
sections.p: Identify precipitating and predisposing factors, prioritising those common in low‑resource tropical settings.

b: Depression: low mood, anhedonia, weight loss, suicidal thoughts
Psychosis: hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech
Anxiety: excessive worry, somatic tension, panic attacks
Substance‑induced: agitation, confusion, withdrawal signs
sections.p: Presentations vary by disorder but share core domains: mood, thought, perception, cognition and behaviour.
Use targeted tests to rule out organic causes; when unavailable, rely on clinical clues.

t.b: Detect anemia or infection that may mimic or worsen psychiatric symptoms; low hemoglobin suggests anemia‑related fatigue.
Identify HIV‑associated neurocognitive disorder; positive result prompts ART optimisation.
Rule out neurosyphilis presenting with psychosis; reactive test warrants lumbar puncture if possible.
Detect stimulant or cannabis intoxication; negative result supports primary psychiatric diagnosis.
Identify structural lesions; if not available, consider referral for severe focal deficits.

b: Suicidal intent with plan or means
Acute psychosis with violence risk
Severe withdrawal (e.g., alcohol delirium tremens)
New neurological deficit suggesting organic brain disease
sections.p: Recognise signs that demand urgent medical attention.

b: First‑line antidepressants: amitriptyline or fluoxetine – chosen for low cost and availability; avoid MAO‑inhibitors due to dietary restrictions.
Antipsychotics: haloperidol (injectable) for acute agitation; avoid high‑dose chlorpromazine in cardiac disease.
Benzodiazepines (lorazepam) for severe anxiety or agitation – short‑term only to prevent dependence.
Psychosocial: brief CBT techniques, problem‑solving therapy, involvement of family and community health workers.
sections.p: Combine pharmacological, psychosocial and community interventions; adapt to drug availability.

b: Re‑assess mood and function every 2‑4 weeks initially
Screen for medication side effects (e.g., anticholinergic burden)
Link patient to support groups, livelihood programmes, and HIV/TB services
sections.p: Plan regular outpatient reviews, monitor treatment response and side effects, and address social determinants.

b: Depression vs. hypothyroidism – check thyroid function if available
Psychosis vs. cerebral malaria – look for fever, recent travel, malaria smear
Anxiety vs. cardiac ischemia – assess chest pain, risk factors, ECG if possible
sections.p: Distinguish psychiatric disorders from medical mimics common in the region.

b: Normal CBC does not exclude HIV‑related neurocognitive disorder
Negative urine toxicology may miss recent khat use (not routinely screened)
Mild anemia can exaggerate fatigue, mimicking depression
sections.p: Interpret laboratory and clinical findings cautiously.

whenToSeekHelp: Acute psychosis with risk of harm
